questions.q: What problem is platform governance actually solving, according to this lesson's recap of Chapter 2's Domain Separation lesson?
options: Walling off each department's data using the sys_domain field
Replacing the integration inventory from Chapter 4 entirely
Eliminating the need for any code review across the instance
Governing how multiple departments are allowed to change a shared platform, which is a process decision, not a data-separation decision like Domain Separation
questions.explain: Most multi-department situations are governance problems, not genuine data-separation requirements — governance is the real, lower-cost alternative Domain Separation's lesson pointed toward.

questions.q: Under centralized governance, what is the honest downside as an organization grows?
options: Integrations duplicate across departments
Every department's request queues behind the same small platform team, and delivery slows exactly as demand increases
Naming conventions become impossible to enforce
There is no honest downside to centralized governance at any scale
questions.explain: Centralized governance's consistency comes at the cost of throughput — one team approving every change becomes a bottleneck as more departments depend on it.

questions.q: What is the real risk of federated governance if guardrails aren't actively maintained?
options: Federated governance has no realistic risk at all
The platform team becomes a bottleneck
Departments independently rebuild integrations and invent contradictory naming or role conventions, producing real inconsistency
Delivery speed drops below what centralized governance would provide
questions.explain: Federated autonomy without guardrails is how duplicate integrations and inconsistent conventions quietly reappear across an instance.

questions.q: Which of these is one of the three guardrails this lesson says makes federated governance survivable?
options: Letting each department choose its own naming convention independently
Turning on Domain Separation for every department
A shared component library, so similar capabilities are built once and reused rather than reinvented per department
Removing all code review to maximize department speed
questions.explain: A shared component library, alongside naming conventions and mandatory code review, is one of the three guardrails that keeps federated autonomy from becoming drift.

questions.q: What does this lesson mean by saying federated governance without guardrails "isn't governance at all"?
options: Autonomy to release without any maintained standard is functionally the same as having no governance model, just more departments making uncoordinated changes
Guardrails are optional once a department has shipped its first change successfully
Federated governance always requires Domain Separation to function
Centralized governance is the only model that counts as real governance
questions.explain: Governance means a deliberate, maintained standard for how changes happen — remove the guardrails and federation collapses into uncoordinated change, not a lighter-weight governance model.
